rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to locate the eight-peak elution window and identify critical separations. The high final organic fraction limits truncation risk, while the moderate temperature leaves room to probe temperature-dependent selectivity.

Keep the gradient fixed and raise temperature to test selectivity changes in the four-peak cluster and the nearly coeluting final pair. All peaks currently elute well before 10 minutes, leaving time headroom for later gradient refinement.

At 60 C, substantially reduce the gradient slope to test whether the remaining close pairs separate through increased retention and altered gradient selectivity. The current 4.71-minute last peak leaves room to improve separation before incurring a time penalty.

Lower temperature by one grid step while preserving the shallower gradient that resolved the earlier cluster. This probes temperature selectivity for the sole remaining critical pair, with some margin before the last peak reaches 10 minutes.

Make the gradient modestly shallower at 55 C to improve the remaining early critical pair while retaining the strong separation of the later peaks. This tests whether full resolution is attainable near the 10-minute elution target.

Return to 60 C to improve the early critical pair, and use a shallower gradient to move the later pair away from its near-coelution condition. Raising the starting organic fraction should help offset the longer gradient’s retention-time cost.

Further reduce the gradient slope at 60 C to separate the remaining later critical pair. Increase the starting organic fraction to counter the retention-time increase and aim to keep the last peak near 10 minutes.

Probe the low-temperature end for a different selectivity regime, since 55–60 C trades separation of the early cluster against the later critical pair. A 20-minute gradient limits the retention-time increase while testing whether the early pair separates on the opposite side of its coelution condition.

Refine the nearly optimal 25 C method with a slightly shallower gradient to improve the marginal R = 1.47 pair. Raising the starting organic fraction should offset the longer gradient and bring the last peak below 10 minutes.

Injection 9 attained the maximum CRF; now shorten the gradient by one step to seek faster elution while preserving full resolution. Its minimum resolution of 1.89 provides some margin for this change.

Restore the 22-minute gradient that achieved full resolution, but raise the starting organic fraction one step to accelerate elution. This tests a different route to a faster method after shortening the gradient reduced the critical pair below R = 1.5.

Test a higher starting organic fraction for faster elution, paired with a shallower gradient to protect the critical separation that is now just above R = 1.5. Retain injection 11 as the fastest fully resolved method demonstrated so far.

Test a one-step temperature increase from the fastest fully resolved method to seek shorter retention and assess selectivity of its marginal pair. Keep the gradient unchanged to isolate the temperature effect.

Test whether the higher-start, shallower gradient restores the early separation lost at 30 C while retaining its faster elution. At 25 C this gradient strengthened the preceding pair, and warming may improve its remaining marginal pair.
Lengthen the gradient one step to improve the sole unresolved pair at R = 1.30. The neighboring critical pairs remain above 1.5, and the 7.70-minute last peak leaves ample time margin.

Lower temperature one step to restore separation of the final pair while retaining the shallower gradient needed by the early cluster. This tests a fully resolved higher-starting-organic method before further time optimization.

Probe 35 C at the gradient used in injections 11 and 13 to test whether temperature-driven elution-order changes open a faster fully resolved window. Injection 11 remains the fastest demonstrated method with maximum CRF.

Test a warmer selectivity window beyond the early-cluster crossover seen at 35 C, keeping the gradient fixed for comparison. The maximum CRF is already secured, so this run seeks a faster fully resolved alternative.

Probe 50 C with a modestly shallower gradient to seek improved early-cluster selectivity and move the later critical pair away from its 45 C condition. The seven-minute elution window leaves substantial room for this refinement.

Return to the more promising 45 C selectivity and reduce the gradient slope to improve its two marginal separations. The previous last peak at 7.03 minutes leaves room for a longer gradient while remaining below the time-penalty threshold.

Lower temperature from injection 20 to move the late pair away from its coelution condition while testing the early cluster at an intermediate temperature. This is a final local search for a faster alternative to the fully resolved 25 C methods.

Return to the successful 25 C selectivity and test a higher starting organic fraction with a substantially shallower gradient to protect the early critical pair. This seeks faster full resolution while retaining injection 11 as the fastest proven maximum-CRF method.

Refine the fastest proven maximum-CRF method using a narrower organic window and a slightly shallower slope. This should add resolution margin to its R = 1.52 critical pair while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes.

Reduce the final organic fraction one step to increase resolution margin around the successful 25 C method. Injection 23 leaves 0.82 minutes before the time penalty, so this modest slope reduction may preserve maximum CRF with stronger critical-pair separation.

Shorten injection 24’s gradient by one step, using its minimum resolution of 2.07 to trade excess separation for faster elution. The resulting slope lies between two demonstrated maximum-CRF methods, making this a conservative final refinement.
